newsitem.title: USA: Columbia/HCA affair damages faith in U.S. healthcare.
newsitem.headline: Columbia/HCA affair damages faith in U.S. healthcare.

text.p: Public trust in the medical establishment suffered another blow Friday with the sudden resignation of the chairman of the largest U.S. for-profit hospital company under the cloud of a massive federal probe.

Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Richard Scott resigned after a late-night meeting Thursday of the company's board, whose members reportedly were unhappy with Scott's handling of the investigation.

Federal agents raided Columbia facilities, seized files and subpoenaed five mid-level executives in recent days in a broad inquiry focused so far on possible improper billing for laboratory tests, home healthcare and Medicare-related work.

The investigation and the resulting shake-up at the top ranks of the Nashville, Tenn.-based company are likely to further erode Americans' faith in the people and institutions that pay for and provide their health care, experts said.

"The public is increasingly sceptical, angry and troubled," said Dr. Rashi Fein, professor of the economics of medicine at Harvard Medical School and a former policy adviser in the Kennedy administration.
"There's anger at employers, there's anger at the HMOs and there is a certain inevitable lack of trust or confusion about what role the physician has," Fein said.

Trust in health care has slipped as people have come to see hospitals and other segments of the industry as more interested in profits than in people, according to a recent study by the American Hospital Association.

The study involved 300 adults in 31 focus groups across the country and found that many people questioned whether health care providers based their decisions on the patient's welfare, or on other considerations.

"There is a small crisis of confidence. People are wondering just whether physicians are making decisions for economic reasons, to help a company or to help themselves," said Clark Bell, editor of Modern Healthcare, a Chicago-based magazine for hospital and health care executives.
Other studies have shown that physicians still are viewed as among the most respected and trusted professionals in the country, but their ranking has fallen.
Paradoxically, people asked for an opinion about their personal physician, however, are more trusting.
"I don't think it has yet come down to a failure to believe in and trust individual practitioners. But I think that is beginning, certainly in the HMO context," Fein said.

Opinions on health care are shifting in response to wrenching changes within the industry, brought on by runaway cost inflation in the 1980s and the rise of health maintenance organisations, or HMOs, and for-profit hospital companies.
Since its founding in 1987, Columbia/HCA has played a major role in restructuring the industry as an aggressive acquirer of hospitals and a tough competitor.

The company today runs 342 hospitals, 150 surgery centres and more than 570 home health locations in 36 states, Britain, Switzerland and Spain. It had 1996 revenues of nearly $20 billion and profits of $1.5 billion.

Under the hard-driving Scott, who was replaced Friday by long-time board member Dr. Thomas Frist, Columbia/HCA stood for efficiency and a bottom-line attitude that irked some in a profession that sees itself as concerned with more than money.
"Everybody loves to hate" Columbia/HCA, said Dr. John Lantos, associate director of the MacLean Centre for Clinical Medical Ethics at the University of Chicago.

There are 5,000 hospitals in the United States. About 15 percent are owned by companies such as Columbia/HCA. The remainder are still non-profit and have their roots in charity, religious or educational institutions.

As long as for-profit companies are involved along with government and non-profit concerns in health care -- and all seem to be here to stay -- conflicts and questions like those now surrounding Columbia/HCA will arise, Lantos said.
Moreover, physicians said, the public will continue to be caught in the confusing middle as the industry struggles to find the proper balance between profit and charity.

"As medicine has become more commercialized, there has been an erosion of trust," said Dr. Gregory Gramelspacher, an associate professor and medical ethicist at the Indiana University School of Medicine in Indianapolis.
"In some sense, it's more important in medicine now to get an MBA than it is to get an MD ... and that's coming back to bite us in the medical profession," Gramelspacher said.
